title: UNIT 5: INTRODUCTION TO ENVIRONMENTAL CHEMISTRY
notes:
✓ Environmental chemistry → Deals with the production, movement, reactions, effects, and fate of chemical substances in the air, water, soil, and living systems.
It also studies how human activities affect the environment and how chemistry can be used to prevent or reduce environmental problems.

title: 5.1 Introduction to Environmental Chemistry
notes:
✓ Environment → Includes all the natural systems and surroundings that support life.
✓ Environmental chemistry → Studies chemical processes occurring in these systems and the effects of human activities on them.

◆ MAJOR ENVIRONMENTAL COMPARTMENTS
Atmosphere
Hydrosphere
Lithosphere
Biosphere

→ These compartments continuously interact with one another through natural chemical and physical processes.

◆ IMPORTANT BIOLOGICAL CHEMICAL PROCESSES
✓ Photosynthesis → Converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using sunlight.
✓ Respiration → Uses glucose and oxygen to release energy and produces carbon dioxide and water.

title: 5.1.1 Components of the Environment
notes:
✓ The environment consists of four major components.

◆ ATMOSPHERE
The layer of gases surrounding Earth. It contains mainly nitrogen and oxygen together with smaller amounts of other gases.

◆ HYDROSPHERE
All water found on Earth, including oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, and water vapor.

◆ LITHOSPHERE
The solid outer part of Earth, including rocks, minerals, and soil.

◆ BIOSPHERE
The part of Earth where living organisms exist and interact with air, water, and land.

→ These components are interconnected. A change in one component can affect the others.

title: 5.1.2 Natural Cycles in the Environment
notes:
✓ Natural cycles → Continuously circulate substances that are essential for life and environmental processes.

◆ IMPORTANT CYCLES
Hydrologic cycle
Oxygen cycle
Nitrogen cycle
Phosphorus cycle
Sulfur cycle
Carbon cycle

◆ HYDROLOGIC CYCLE
Water continuously moves between the atmosphere, land, surface water, and groundwater through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, and runoff.

◆ OXYGEN CYCLE
Oxygen moves through the atmosphere, organisms, water, and minerals. Photosynthesis produces oxygen, while respiration and combustion consume oxygen.

◆ NITROGEN CYCLE
Nitrogen moves between the atmosphere, soil, plants, animals, and microorganisms. Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric nitrogen into forms that can be used by organisms.

◆ CARBON CYCLE
Plants remove CO₂ from the atmosphere through photosynthesis. Carbon returns through respiration, decomposition, and combustion of fossil fuels.

◆ SULFUR AND PHOSPHORUS CYCLES
These cycles move sulfur and phosphorus through rocks, soil, water, organisms, and the atmosphere, supporting important biological and chemical processes.

title: 5.1.3 Concepts Related to Environmental Chemistry
notes:
◆ POLLUTANT
✓ Pollutant → A substance whose concentration has increased due to human activity and produces harmful effects on the environment.
Examples include SO₂, CO₂, O₃, lead, mercury, excess heat, light, and sound.

◆ CONTAMINANT
✓ Contaminant → A substance introduced into the environment that can become a pollutant when it produces harmful effects.

◆ SINK
✓ Sink → A medium that interacts with pollutants and retains them or converts them chemically.

◆ DISSOLVED OXYGEN (DO)
✓ DO → Oxygen dissolved in water. It is essential for aquatic life.
Good-quality water generally contains about 4–8 mg/L of dissolved oxygen.

◆ BIOLOGICAL OXYGEN DEMAND (BOD)
✓ BOD → A measure of the oxygen consumed by microorganisms when decomposing dissolved organic matter in water.
It is determined by comparing dissolved oxygen before and after a specified incubation period.

◆ THRESHOLD LIMIT VALUE (TLV)
✓ TLV → The permissible concentration of a toxic pollutant to which a healthy person may be exposed during an 8-hour working day without harmful effects.

title: 5.2 Environmental Pollution
notes:
✓ Pollution → The discharge of solid, liquid, or gaseous substances, or radiation, into the environment in a way that causes unwanted changes and harms ecological balance or quality of life.

✓ Pollutant sources → May include natural events such as volcanic eruptions, as well as human activities including industry, transportation, agriculture, mining, and improper waste disposal.

◆ THREE MAJOR TYPES
Air pollution
Water pollution
Land pollution

title: 5.2.1 Air Pollution
notes:
✓ Air pollution → Caused by harmful or contaminating substances present in the atmosphere that affect living organisms and the environment.

◆ COMMON AIR POLLUTANTS
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂)
Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)
Carbon monoxide (CO)
Ozone (O₃)
Hydrocarbons
Particulate matter
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
Lead compounds

◆ MAJOR SOURCES
Combustion of fossil fuels
Industrial processes
Vehicle exhaust
Mining
Other human activities

✓ Acid rain → SO₂ and nitrogen oxides can react with water in the atmosphere to form acids and contribute to acid rain.

→ Acid rain can damage vegetation, aquatic ecosystems, buildings, metals, and soil.

◆ REDUCTION METHODS
Cleaner fuels
Emission-control technologies
Improved industrial processes
Public transportation
Renewable energy
Proper regulation of emissions

title: 5.2.2 Water Pollution
notes:
✓ Water pollution → Degradation of water quality caused by the discharge of harmful substances into rivers, lakes, groundwater, oceans, and other water bodies.

◆ MAJOR SOURCES
Untreated sewage
Industrial waste
Agricultural runoff
Fertilizers
Pesticides
Detergents
Oil spills
Heavy metals

✓ Excess nitrate and phosphate → Can promote excessive growth of aquatic plants and algae.
✓ Organic wastes → Can consume dissolved oxygen during decomposition.
✓ Low dissolved oxygen → Can harm or kill aquatic organisms.

◆ REDUCTION METHODS
Wastewater treatment
Proper disposal of industrial and domestic wastes
Controlled fertilizer use
Prevention of oil spills
Recycling
Protection of water sources

title: 5.2.3 Land Pollution
notes:
✓ Land pollution → Occurs when harmful substances accumulate on or in the soil and reduce its quality or usefulness.

◆ MAJOR CAUSES
Improper disposal of garbage
Plastics
Industrial waste
Oil spills
Harmful chemicals
Heavy metals
Excessive use of synthetic fertilizers

✓ Non-biodegradable materials → Plastics, glass, electronic components, and some synthetic materials can remain in the environment for long periods.

→ Their accumulation can interfere with air and water movement in soil and affect plant growth.

◆ REDUCTION METHODS
Proper waste collection and disposal
Reuse
Recycling
Composting
Controlled use of fertilizers and pesticides
Safe management of hazardous wastes

title: 5.3 Global Warming and Climate Change
notes:
✓ Global warming → The long-term increase in Earth's average temperature.
✓ Climate change → Broader long-term changes in temperature, rainfall, weather patterns, and other climate characteristics.

◆ HUMAN ACTIVITIES CONTRIBUTING TO CLIMATE CHANGE
Burning fossil fuels
Deforestation
Industrial processes
Agriculture
Waste management

✓ Greenhouse gases → Human activities can increase their concentration in the atmosphere.

✓ Carbon dioxide → An important contributor released from fossil-fuel combustion and other activities.

◆ OTHER GREENHOUSE GASES
Methane
Nitrous oxide
Ozone
Water vapor
Fluorinated gases

→ Climate change can affect ecosystems, agriculture, water resources, weather patterns, sea levels, and human societies.

title: 5.3.1 Greenhouse Effect
notes:
✓ Greenhouse effect → The warming of Earth caused by gases in the atmosphere that absorb infrared radiation and prevent some heat from escaping into space.

✓ Natural greenhouse effect → Essential for maintaining Earth's temperature.
✓ Enhanced greenhouse effect → Increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases can strengthen the greenhouse effect and contribute to global warming.

◆ IMPORTANT GREENHOUSE GASES
Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
Methane (CH₄)
Nitrous oxide (N₂O)
Ozone (O₃)
Water vapor (H₂O)
Fluorinated gases

→ Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of the atmosphere but do not significantly absorb infrared radiation in the way greenhouse gases do.

title: 5.3.2 Chemistry of Greenhouse Gases and Climate Change
notes:
✓ Greenhouse gases → Absorb infrared radiation and transfer energy within the atmosphere, contributing to warming.

◆ CARBON DIOXIDE SOURCES
Combustion of fossil fuels
Deforestation
Cement production
Other processes

◆ METHANE SOURCES
Livestock
Agriculture
Waste
Fossil-fuel production
Other sources

◆ NITROUS OXIDE SOURCES
Agricultural activities
Industrial activities

✓ General combustion of hydrocarbons:
CₓHᵧ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + heat

✓ CFCs and other fluorinated compounds → Can affect atmospheric chemistry.
CFCs can contribute to depletion of the ozone layer when they reach the upper atmosphere and undergo reactions initiated by ultraviolet radiation.

◆ REDUCTION APPROACHES
Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions
Improving energy efficiency
Using renewable energy
Protecting forests
Developing cleaner technologies

title: 5.4 Green Chemistry and Cleaner Production
notes:
✓ Green chemistry → Aims to make chemical products and processes safer and more environmentally sustainable.

→ Instead of producing pollution and treating it afterward, green chemistry focuses on preventing pollution during the design and production of chemicals.

✓ Life-cycle approach → A green process considers the entire life cycle of a product, from raw materials and production to use and final disposal.

✓ Cleaner production → Aims to reduce waste, hazardous substances, energy consumption, and environmental impacts while improving efficiency and sustainability.

title: 5.4.1 Principles of Green Chemistry
notes:
✓ The 12 principles of green chemistry provide guidelines for designing safer and more sustainable chemical processes.

◆ 1. PREVENTION
Prevent waste rather than treating it afterward.

◆ 2. ATOM ECONOMY
Maximize incorporation of reactant atoms into the desired product.

◆ 3. LESS HAZARDOUS CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS
Reduce the use and generation of hazardous substances.

◆ 4. DESIGN SAFER CHEMICALS
Make products effective but less harmful.

◆ 5. SAFER SOLVENTS AND AUXILIARIES
Use safer solvents or avoid them when possible.

◆ 6. ENERGY EFFICIENCY
Reduce energy requirements and favor mild conditions.

◆ 7. RENEWABLE FEEDSTOCKS
Use renewable raw materials where possible.

◆ 8. REDUCE DERIVATIVES
Avoid unnecessary chemical modifications.

◆ 9. CATALYSIS
Use catalysts to improve efficiency and reduce waste.

◆ 10. DESIGN FOR DEGRADATION
Products should break down into harmless substances after use.

◆ 11. REAL-TIME ANALYSIS
Monitor processes to prevent pollution as it occurs.

◆ 12. INHERENTLY SAFER CHEMISTRY
Choose substances and processes that reduce the chance of accidents.

title: 5.4.2 Cleaner Production in Chemistry
notes:
✓ Cleaner production → Focuses on preventing waste and pollution at the source rather than cleaning them up after they are produced.

◆ IDEAL CHEMICAL PROCESS
Safety
Simplicity
Selectivity
High yield
Energy efficiency
Renewable or recyclable raw materials
Minimal hazardous by-products

◆ ATOM ECONOMY
✓ Atom economy → Measures how effectively reactant atoms are incorporated into the desired product.

% Atom economy = (Formula mass of desired product ÷ Sum of formula masses of all reactants) × 100

✓ High atom economy → Most reactant atoms become part of the desired product, producing less waste.

→ Cleaner production can reduce the use of raw materials, energy, hazardous chemicals, and waste-treatment costs while reducing environmental pollution.

title: UNIT 5 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ ENVIRONMENTAL CHEMISTRY → Study of chemical substances and processes in the environment and their interactions with human activities.

✓ ENVIRONMENT → Atmosphere + Hydrosphere + Lithosphere + Biosphere.

✓ POLLUTANT → Substance whose increased concentration due to human activity causes harmful environmental effects.

✓ POLLUTION → Unwanted environmental change caused by substances or energy entering the environment.

◆ THREE TYPES OF POLLUTION
Air pollution
Water pollution
Land pollution

✓ DO → Dissolved oxygen in water; important for aquatic life.
✓ BOD → Oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing organic matter in water.
✓ GREENHOUSE EFFECT → Warming caused by atmospheric gases absorbing infrared radiation.
✓ GLOBAL WARMING → Long-term increase in Earth's average temperature.
✓ GREENHOUSE GASES → CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, O₃, H₂O, and fluorinated gases.
✓ GREEN CHEMISTRY → Designing chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and pollution.
✓ ATOM ECONOMY → Measures how efficiently reactant atoms become part of the desired product.
✓ CLEANER PRODUCTION → Preventing waste and pollution at the source through safer, more efficient, and sustainable processes.
